title: "STRASSE".lower() is not "straße" — uppercasing and lowercasing aren't inverses
assumption: If a.upper() == b, then a == b.lower().

input.description: A German street name or surname containing ß, compared against an all-caps form from a passport, an old database export, or a form that forces uppercase input.

what_goes_wrong: "stra\u00dfe".upper() correctly equals "STRASSE", but "STRASSE".lower() comes back as "strasse", not "stra\u00dfe" — so the round trip breaks and a plain .lower()-keyed uniqueness check treats the two spellings as different strings.
why: Unicode's default full uppercase mapping of ß is the two letters "SS" (a capital ẞ, U+1E9E, exists but is not the default mapping), which is why "stra\u00dfe".upper() == "STRASSE" and why this case operation changes string length. The mapping only goes one way: lowercasing "SS" gives "ss", because plenty of words have a real double s. Python's str.casefold() (added in Python 3.3) applies Unicode case folding, which maps ß to "ss", so casefold() == casefold() succeeds where lower() == lower() fails. JavaScript has no casefold(); toLowerCase() and toUpperCase() show the same asymmetry, and the built-in caseless comparison is Intl.Collator or localeCompare with sensitivity "base", which treats "straße" and "STRASSE" as equal.

repros.code:
a = "STRASSE"
b = "stra\u00dfe"
print(b.upper() == a, a.lower() == b)
print(a.casefold() == b.casefold())
print("\u00df".upper(), len("\u00df".upper()))

fix: For caseless comparison, use Python's str.casefold() rather than str.lower(). In JavaScript, compare with new Intl.Collator(undefined, { sensitivity: "base" }).compare(a, b) === 0 (note that "base" also ignores accents), or normalize ß to "ss" explicitly before comparing. For stored uniqueness keys, also normalize (NFKC or NFC) before folding.

sources.title: Unicode Standard: SpecialCasing.txt (ß → SS uppercase mapping)
Unicode Technical Standard #10 / TR21: Case Mappings

test_cases.note: A caseless-match key should map both to the same value (Python's casefold() does; lower() does not).
